title: A short Python bridge
goal: Read the small amount of Python needed to begin the pandas lessons.
prerequisites: No programming experience is required; work through one line at a time.

cells.title: Names hold values
cells.explanation: A variable is a name associated with a value. The equals sign assigns a value; two equals signs compare values. Quotation marks make text, while an unquoted number can take part in arithmetic. print() displays a value so you can inspect it.
cells.code:
name = "Amira"
age = 20
next_age = age + 1
is_twenty = age == 20
print(name)
print(next_age)
print(is_twenty)
print(type(age).__name__)

questions.prompt: Which line assigns a value, and which line compares two values?
questions.answer: age = 20 assigns 20 to age. The expression age == 20 compares age with 20 and produces True.

questions.prompt: What will next_age print? Will age itself become 21?
questions.answer: next_age prints 21. age stays 20 because the calculated value was assigned to a different name.
"20" is text; 20 is a whole number. Their types determine which operations make sense.

cells.task: Describe Bilal, age 21, using name and age. Calculate his age in three years in next_age. Store the comparison of his current age with 21 in is_twenty_one, then print the results.
cells.hint: Change the name and starting age, then use age + 3. Keep = for assignment and == for comparison.
cells.solution:
name = "Bilal"
age = 21
next_age = age + 3
is_twenty_one = age == 21
print(name)
print(next_age)
print(is_twenty_one)
cells.solution_note: The results are Bilal, 24, and True. The original age remains 21.

check.feedback: The double equals sign compares two values. A single equals sign assigns a value.

cells.verify:
assert name == 'Amira' and age == 20
assert next_age == 21 and is_twenty is True
cells.solution_verify:
assert name == 'Bilal' and age == 21
assert next_age == 24 and is_twenty_one is True
cells.watch: Python names are case-sensitive: age and Age are different names.
cells.takeaway: I can distinguish a value, a variable, an assignment, and a comparison.

cells.title: A list keeps values in order
cells.explanation: Square brackets create a list. Each value has a position, beginning at 0. len() counts the values, and a slice selects a range of positions. A slice includes its start position and excludes its stop position.
cells.code:
scores = [88, 72, 91]
first_score = scores[0]
first_two = scores[0:2]
print(first_score)
print(first_two)
print(len(scores))

questions.prompt: What is the difference between scores and scores[0]?
questions.answer: scores is the whole list. scores[0] retrieves the first value, 88.

questions.prompt: Does scores[0:2] contain two values or three?
questions.answer: Two values: 88 and 72. Position 2 is excluded from the slice.

questions.prompt: Why would scores[3] fail for this list?
questions.answer: The list has three values at positions 0, 1, and 2. Position 3 does not exist, so Python raises IndexError.

cells.task: Select the second and third scores into result. Then add 65 to the end of scores using append(), and print the new list length.
cells.solution:
scores = [88, 72, 91]
result = scores[1:3]
scores.append(65)
print(result)
print(scores)
print(len(scores))
cells.solution_note: result contains 72 and 91. The original list now has four values, ending in 65.

check.prompt: Which position refers to the first list value?
check.feedback: Python list positions begin at zero.

cells.verify:
assert scores == [88, 72, 91]
assert first_score == 88 and first_two == [88, 72]
cells.watch: A list position is an integer. The text "0" is not the same as position 0.
cells.takeaway: I can count, select, and append list values.

cells.title: Give a calculation a name
cells.explanation: A function is a named set of instructions you can reuse. def starts a function definition, and the indented body states what it does. A parameter receives an input value when the function is called. return sends the result back so it can be saved or used in another calculation.
cells.code:
def add_bonus(score, bonus):
    return score + bonus

first = add_bonus(72, 3)
second = add_bonus(88, 2)
print(first)
print(second)

questions.prompt: In add_bonus(72, 3), what values do score and bonus receive?
questions.answer: score receives 72 and bonus receives 3 for that call.

questions.prompt: What do first and second contain?
Why return the answer instead of only printing it inside the function?
questions.answer: A returned answer can be saved in a variable and used later. Printing alone displays it but does not return that answer to the caller.

cells.task: Create a function called to_percentage(points, maximum) that returns points divided by maximum, multiplied by 100. Calculate 16 out of 20 into result and print it.
cells.hint: Keep the return line indented. For this exercise, maximum is positive.
cells.solution:
def to_percentage(points, maximum):
    return (points / maximum) * 100

result = to_percentage(16, 20)
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The returned percentage is 80.0. The same function can be called with a different number of points and a different positive maximum.

check.prompt: Which keyword sends the calculated answer back to the caller?
check.feedback: return supplies the function's result. def defines a function; print displays information.

cells.verify:
assert first == 75 and second == 90
assert add_bonus(10, 0) == 10
cells.watch: Indentation is part of Python syntax. Division also requires a nonzero denominator.
cells.takeaway: I can read a small function, call it, and use its returned value.

cells.title: Import a tool and read an error
cells.explanation: import makes a module's tools available; as gives the module a shorter name. This example uses Python's built-in math module. The try/except block catches an expected conversion error so we can read its type and message, then continue. Read the error name and the failing value before changing code.
cells.code:
import math as m

try:
    number = float("nine")
except ValueError as error:
    print(type(error).__name__ + ": " + str(error))

number = float("9")
result = m.sqrt(number)
print("Corrected result:", result)

questions.prompt: What does m refer to after import math as m?
questions.answer: m is a short name for the math module. m.sqrt accesses its square-root function.

questions.prompt: Why does float("nine") raise ValueError, but float("9") works?
questions.answer: The word nine cannot be parsed as a numeric value by float. The digit string 9 can, producing 9.0.

questions.prompt: What should you inspect first when a cell reports an error?
questions.answer: Read the error type, its message, and the line that failed. Check the actual input and variable names rather than changing unrelated lines.

cells.task: Import math as m, set text to "25", convert text to a number, and calculate its square root in result. Print the result.
cells.hint: Use float(text) for conversion and m.sqrt(number) for the calculation.
cells.solution:
import math as m

text = "25"
number = float(text)
result = m.sqrt(number)
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The result is 5.0. Later, import pandas as pd follows the same alias pattern; pandas supplies the data tools used in the course.

check.prompt: What does as pd mean in import pandas as pd?
options: Use pd as a short name for the pandas module
Convert every value to a number
check.feedback: The alias pd refers to the imported pandas module, which is why pd.Series and pd.DataFrame work.

cells.verify:
assert number == 9.0 and result == 3.0
assert m.sqrt(16) == 4.0
cells.solution_verify: assert text == '25' and number == 25.0 and result == 5.0
cells.watch: Catching an error does not repair its cause. This example prints the expected error and then supplies a valid value explicitly.
cells.takeaway: I can recognize an import alias and use an error message to guide a correction.
